title: Shams disappears
hook: Shams leaves, returns, and vanishes for good around 1247, and Rumi's grief becomes poetry

segments.voice: Yesterday, a stranger from Tabriz grabbed a scholar's bridle in the market. Your line was someone arrives. Who did you really listen to? Day one hundred sixty-one.

You've probably seen someone grieve out loud. Not quietly, not politely. The friend who played the same song forty times after the breakup. The widower who talked about his wife to everyone at the grocery store. Grief that has to go somewhere. Rumi's life had just been turned upside down by a friend. Then the friend left. Then he came back. Then, one winter night around 1247, he was gone, and nobody ever saw him again. The respectable scholar did something no one in Konya expected. He began to sing. Today, Shams disappears.
screen: `GRIEF THAT HAS TO GO SOMEWHERE.` → `GONE, AROUND 1247.` → `SHAMS DISAPPEARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as the sources give it. Rumi's students resented Shams for taking their teacher away. After about sixteen months, in early 1246, Shams slipped out of Konya and went to Damascus. Rumi was desolate. He sent his son Sultan Walad all the way to Syria to bring him back, and Shams came. For a while things were good. Then the resentment returned, and around December 1247 Shams vanished for good. What happened? Honestly, nobody knows. A later story says he was murdered, and even names one of Rumi's own sons as involved. Many historians think that story is doubtful, and there's no proof. Other accounts say he simply left, as he'd left places all his life. Rumi went looking. He traveled to Damascus, searching the streets. And somewhere in the search, the tradition says, he stopped looking outside. He began to feel that what he loved in Shams was already speaking through him. And he wrote. Out of this loss came a huge collection of lyric poems, thousands of them, often composed aloud, some while he turned to music. It's called the Divan of Shams of Tabriz, because at the end of many poems, where a poet usually signs his own name, Rumi signed his friend's. Think about that. He gave his poems away to the one he'd lost. Grief didn't go quiet in him. It became music. That's what your line means: the grief sang.
screen: `SHAMS LEAVES FOR DAMASCUS.` · `BROUGHT BACK, THEN GONE FOR GOOD.` · `NOBODY KNOWS WHAT HAPPENED.` · `POEMS SIGNED WITH HIS FRIEND'S NAME.` · then, large: `THE GRIEF SANG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line for someone gone. Let one person come to mind: someone who died, moved away, or drifted off. Settle, and breathe with them near. Then find one line. It doesn't have to be poetry. It can be a thing they used to say, or what you'd tell them now, or just their name and a color. Say it inside, or write it down. Let the missing be there without fixing it. The bell holds the time.
Shams disappears. Around 1247 Rumi's friend vanished for good, and Rumi's grief poured out as thousands of poems signed with Shams's name. Today's word.
Your line: the grief sang. Today, keep the line you wrote with you, and read it once more tonight, out loud if you can. Day one hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Readers of Rumi usually meet this grief through the Divan of Shams of Tabriz, his collection of lyric poems, many of which close with Shams's name where a poet would sign his own.

original.note: Persian: a collected book of poems. the Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi is Rumi's lyric collection.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rumi wrote love poems.
what it means: much of his lyric poetry grew from grief for a friend who disappeared.
what a scholar hears: the Divan-e Shams, thousands of ghazals, often signed with Shams's name in the closing line where a poet's own pen name belongs.

notes: Chronology: Shams in Konya about sixteen months, leaves early 1246 (March), brought back by Sultan Walad in 1247, disappears around December 1247. Confirm.
The murder story (involving Rumi's son Ala al-Din) comes from later sources; the script says many historians doubt it and there's no proof. Confirm the hedge.
Rumi's search in Damascus: sources say one or two journeys; script says only 'he traveled to Damascus'. Confirm.
'Thousands' of ghazals: the Divan has roughly 3,000 ghazals plus quatrains. Confirm. Signing with Shams's name (takhallus) is common but not universal in the Divan.
Rumi composing aloud while turning to music (sama): confirm the hedge 'some while he turned to music'.
